name: Accuracy nudge: sharing COVID-19 headlines
author: Human Not Found
description: Original study: Pennycook, G., McPhetres, J., Zhang, Y., Lu, J. G., & Rand, D. G. (2020). Fighting COVID-19 misinformation on social media: Experimental evidence for a scalable accuracy-nudge intervention. Psychological Science, 31(7), 770-780. Across two studies with more than 1,700 US adults, people were worse at telling true from false COVID-19 headlines when deciding what to share than when judging accuracy; in Study 2, asking people to judge the accuracy of a single unrelated headline first nearly tripled truth discernment in their sharing intentions. This template follows Study 2 with ten US participants: in the treatment condition they first rate the accuracy of one non-COVID headline, in the control condition they answer a neutral question instead (the original control had no first task), and both then rate how likely they would be to share each of ten COVID-19 headlines (five true, five false) on a 6-point scale. The headlines are new, written for this template from claims circulating in March 2020. Sharing discernment is the mean of true minus false items; compare it between the conditions. Participants are simulated: each is a Model participant, using the free test model until you choose a model, so the first runs only check the design; with the test model every participant takes the sample answer.

value.prompt: How many hours a day do you usually spend on social media? 1 = less than one hour, 4 = more than three hours.

research.question: Does a prompt to think about accuracy improve truth discernment in sharing?

items.prompt: To the best of your knowledge, how accurate is this headline? "Scientists confirm that the Moon has water ice in craters at its south pole" 1 = not at all accurate, 4 = very accurate.

config.prompt: Before the main task, please answer this question.
